newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German jobless hits record, no relief seen.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German jobless hits record, no relief seen.

text.p: German unemployment climbed to a post-unification record in November as economic recovery failed to boost the labour market and there is no relief in sight, the Federal Labour Office said on Thursday.
The number of unemployed rose 50,000 to a seasonally adjusted 4.1 million, and the adjusted unemployment rate jumped to 10.7 percent from 10.6 percent in October.
The rise, while expected at the start of winter, was larger than many economists had forecast.
"It's really quite substantially more than expected," James Stewart of SE Banken in London told Reuters Financial Television. "It's really unclear in which direction the economy is headed."
Economic growth in the third quarter picked up to 2.4 percent year-on-year, according to official data, but is expected to slow again in the final quarter of the year.

Labour Office President Bernhard Jagoda told a news conference growth would have to be 2.5 to 3.0 percent to turn around the German labour market, which is dogged by structural problems and high wage costs.
"Recovery and growth still don't have the strength to stop the unfavourable development in the labour market," he said.
Ottmar Schreiner, parliamentary labour spokesman for the opposition Social Democrats, said, "The gradual improvement in the economy is bypassing the labour market entirely."

Ursula Engelen-Kefer, deputy head of the Confederation of German Trade Unions (DBG), said anger was rising at the austerity measures European governments were introducing ahead of economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999. Such budget cutting at a time of rising unemployment could spark strikes and social unrest across Europe, she said.
"We need EMU. But it depends how it is shaped. If it is done the way (German finance minister Theo) Waigel wants it...there is the risk of huge strikes," Engelen-Kefer told journalists.

On an unadjusted basis, the number of Germans out of work rose to 3.942 million in November from 3.867 million. Referring to the unadjusted data, Jagoda said he expected the total to rise above four million for the next few months.
German companies are trying to boost competitiveness by raising productivity, doing more with fewer people.
"Strong nominal wage growth and a high level of the real exchange rate is probably forcing employers to reduce employment more aggressively," said Robert Prior-Wandesforde at HSBC James Capel.
Some economists insisted the labour market outlook was gloomy, as growth is expected to taper off in the fourth quarter before possibly heading higher next year.

"The production data for October and now the unemployment rate for November...show that the recovery is only export driven, and will flatten out in the next quarter and next year," said Christian Sobotta of LGT in Frankfurt.

But others were more sanguine. Michael Klawitter of WestLB in Duesseldorf said, "The labour market is a lagging indicator for the economy, so I'm still convinced that the recovery is on track. I would say that overall we should not have a too pessimistic view on the German economy."
In west Germany, the number out of work on a seasonally adjusted basis rose 34,000 to 2.942 million, while east Germany the number of jobless rose 17,000 to to 1.176 million.

Stewart of SE Banken said, "As we move into next year we would expect exports to pick up as the global economy gathers momentum. There is excessive dependence on exports, but that is not unusual for the German economy."
